A: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) targets low loss throughout a weight neighborhood, with weight regularization, rather than at a single parameter setting. A PAC-Bayesian bound connects population loss to worst-case neighborhood training loss and a norm penalty, assuming Gaussian perturbations do not reduce population loss on average and L2 weight norm is at least one; it motivates, but does not certify, the minibatch implementation. SAM approximates the worst-case perturbation using the training gradient, then updates from the gradient at perturbed weights, omitting second-order terms and requiring two backpropagations. Across CIFAR-10/100 configurations, SAM improves over baselines allowed up to twice as many epochs; AutoAugment WideResNet error falls from 2.2% to 1.6% on CIFAR-10, supporting benefits beyond longer pointwise-loss training. Gains extend to ImageNet and EfficientNet finetuning, including 0.30% CIFAR-10 error with ImageNet-plus-JFT-pretrained EfficientNet-L2. Lower Hessian curvature supports the neighborhood-loss rationale. Independent subset perturbations change the effective objective; smaller subsets improve SAM generalization and m-sharpness's predictive value for generalization gaps in the studied settings. Under random label corruption, clean-test accuracy improves, although SAM trails MentorMix and bootstrapping still leaves a deficit at the highest noise rate. One augmented SVHN configuration worsens.
B: Training loss at a single parameter vector can conceal differences in test performance among minima. Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) instead minimizes worst-case loss in a weight neighborhood with weight regularization, favoring solutions whose nearby parameters also have low loss. A PAC-Bayesian bound motivates this objective when Gaussian perturbations do not reduce population loss and the parameter norm is at least one; it does not certify the practical approximation. SAM perturbs weights along the gradient and updates using the perturbed-weight gradient, dropping second-order terms and requiring two backpropagations. On CIFAR-10/100, gains over baselines allowed up to twice as many epochs support benefits beyond longer pointwise training: AutoAugment WideResNet reduces CIFAR-10 error from 2.2% to 1.6%. ImageNet training and pretrained EfficientNet finetuning also improve. Clean-test accuracy improves under random label corruption, but SAM trails MentorMix; bootstrapping narrows the gap without eliminating it at the highest noise rate. Complementary analyses find lower Hessian curvature and show that separate neighborhood maximizations on smaller subsets improve SAM generalization and make m-sharpness more predictive of generalization gaps in the studied settings. These diagnostics support neighborhood-based optimization without establishing curvature as the isolated cause, and an augmented SVHN configuration worsens.

A: Similar training losses can conceal different generalization performance, so Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) targets low loss throughout a parameter neighborhood. A conditional PAC-Bayesian bound motivates worst-case neighborhood-loss minimization, assuming Gaussian perturbations do not reduce population loss and weight norm is at least one. The practical optimizer constructs a loss-increasing perturbation from one gradient, then updates the original weights using a second gradient at the perturbed weights. CIFAR models trained from scratch improve across all tested configurations despite non-SAM baselines being allowed twice as many epochs: AutoAugment WideResNet CIFAR-10 error falls from 2.2% to 1.6%. Gains on ImageNet ResNets and EfficientNet finetuning after ImageNet or ImageNet-plus-JFT pretraining extend this evidence beyond one training regime. Lower Hessian curvature in the tested model supports the intended neighborhood geometry, without establishing a generalization guarantee for approximate updates. With random label noise, SAM improves clean-test accuracy over SGD but trails MentorMix without bootstrapping; an augmented SVHN configuration also worsens. A complementary m-sharpness analysis maximizes loss separately over data subsets: smaller subsets tend to improve generalization and better predict generalization gaps in the evaluated settings, making subset size consequential rather than an implementation detail.
B: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) addresses training minima with similar losses but different test performance by optimizing the worst training loss within a parameter neighborhood. A conditional PAC-Bayesian bound motivates the objective, assuming Gaussian weight perturbations do not lower population loss and Euclidean weight norm is at least one, without certifying approximate minibatch updates. The practical optimizer uses one gradient to choose a loss-increasing perturbation and another at perturbed weights to update the original parameters. Across tested CIFAR configurations, SAM improves generalization even when non-SAM baselines can train for twice as many epochs, supporting a benefit beyond longer point-loss optimization. Lower measured Hessian curvature in the tested model also supports the intended neighborhood geometry. Gains extend to ImageNet ResNets and EfficientNet finetuning after ImageNet or ImageNet-plus-JFT pretraining. Under random label noise, unbootstrapped SAM improves clean-test accuracy over SGD but trails reported MentorMix results; one augmented SVHN configuration regresses. A complementary analysis evaluates sharpness through separate loss maximizations on subsets, defining m-sharpness. Smaller subsets improve generalization in the studied training setting and predict generalization gaps better than full-training-set sharpness.

A: VoxPoser turns language-specified manipulation subtasks into spatial objectives by assigning voxel values that attract an end-effector, object, or object part toward goals and repel it from obstacles. Generated programs query visual perception to ground these maps, letting motion planners optimize desired motion and constraints jointly instead of requiring language models to specify action parameters directly. Observation-based replanning enables zero-shot execution without additional training. Across five real-world tasks, success is 88% in static scenes and 70% under disturbances, versus 24% and 0% for an LLM using simple primitives, supporting spatial composition over sequential primitive specification. Across 13 simulated tasks, category averages favor VoxPoser on seen and unseen instructions and attributes, although individual tasks favor baselines. For three simulated contact-rich tasks, synthesized trajectories also restrict exploration to locally perturbed waypoints: online dynamics learning raises success from 3.3-18.3% to 80.0-91.7% with mean interaction times below three minutes, while exploration without priors exceeds 12 hours. This contrast supports task-directed adaptation when zero-shot plans are insufficient; perception errors, restricted environment dynamics, and end-effector-only planning delimit the demonstrated capabilities.
B: VoxPoser translates language-specified manipulation subtasks into spatial objectives, allowing motion planning to combine desired motions and avoidance constraints rather than relying on sequential action primitives. Language-model-generated programs query visual perception and assign values to three-dimensional locations for an end-effector, object, or object part; planners optimize trajectories against these maps and replan from observations without additional training. Across five real-world tabletop tasks, success reaches 88% in static scenes and 70% under disturbances, versus 24% and 0% for an LLM using simple primitives. This comparison supports spatially composed objectives as an executable alternative to direct primitive parameterization, including when observations change. Across 13 simulated tasks, category averages favor VoxPoser on seen and unseen instruction/attribute splits, although individual tasks sometimes favor baselines. For contact-rich tasks, synthesized trajectories additionally focus exploration near task-relevant interactions for online dynamics learning. On three simulated tasks, this raises success from 3.3-18.3% zero-shot to 80.0-91.7%, with mean interaction times below three minutes, whereas learning without priors exceeds 12 hours. Thus, trajectories insufficient for zero-shot completion can still guide adaptation; perception errors, restricted environment dynamics, and end-effector-only planning delimit the demonstrated scope.

A: VoxPoser turns language-specified manipulation goals into trajectory objectives: pretrained language models generate programs that query perception and assign voxel values attracting an end-effector or object toward targets while discouraging constraint violations. Scoring trajectories against these spatial objectives lets a planner consider goals and constraints jointly instead of encoding them only as primitive sequences, and replan from updated observations without additional training. Across five tabletop robot tasks, success averages 88% without disturbances and 70% with disturbances, versus 24% and 0% for a language-model-plus-primitives baseline, supporting spatial planning for tasks and disruptions that primitive sequencing handles poorly. In 13 simulated tasks, category-level gains over this baseline and learned costmaps extend to unseen instructions and attributes, but individual tasks do not uniformly improve. For contact-intensive simulated door, window, and fridge tasks, zero-shot trajectories are insufficient yet provide exploration priors: sampling near them concentrates interactions around task-relevant motions, enabling dynamics learning with under three minutes of online interaction versus exceeding a twelve-hour limit without priors. Perception and environment dynamics limit performance; prompts remain manually engineered, and planning covers the end-effector rather than the whole arm.
B: VoxPoser turns language-specified manipulation subtasks into spatial objectives, allowing motion planning to satisfy affordances and constraints jointly rather than sequence predefined actions. Pretrained language models generate programs that query visual perception and compose three-dimensional voxel maps; planners optimize trajectories against these maps and replan from updated observations without additional training. Across five tabletop robot tasks, success averages 88% without disturbances and 70% with disturbances, versus 24% and 0% for a language-model-plus-primitives baseline. This comparison supports spatial composition as an alternative to primitive sequencing for these tasks, including disturbed execution. Category-level gains over that baseline and learned costmaps on 13 simulated tasks support transfer to unseen instructions and attributes, but task-level improvements are uneven. For contact-intensive simulated door, window, and fridge tasks, zero-shot trajectories alone are insufficient; using them as exploration priors concentrates action sampling near relevant interactions. Dynamics learning then takes under three minutes of online interaction, whereas exploration without priors exceeds a twelve-hour limit, supporting the trajectories' additional role in guiding learning for contact-intensive tasks. The approach depends on manually supplied prompt examples and perception, and its implementation plans end-effector rather than whole-arm trajectories.
